The spirited comments were the first public statements from the second-term governor about the allegations since his arrest December 9 on federal corruption charges. Blagojevich did not take questions from reporters. Earlier Friday, his attorney, Ed Genson, said he did not feel it was prudent for the governor to answer questions now. The 76-page criminal complaint against Blagojevich includes snippets of intercepted phone calls involving the governor's alleged efforts to benefit from the Senate vacancy. After Blagojevich's statement, Genson's co-counsel, Sam Adam Jr., told reporters that the U.S. attorney's office has not provided them with information related to the criminal complaint. "We've been asking for the documents. We've been asking for the tapes. We've been asking for the witnesses, we're asking for a witness list. We have not gotten that," he said. Blagojevich asserted that he was eager to demonstrate his innocence but insisted he would reserve his defense for the appropriate legal venue. "I'm not going to do what my accusers and political enemies have been doing, and that is talk about this case in 30-second sound bites on 'Meet the Press' or on the TV news," he said. "I have on my side the most powerful ally there is, and it is the truth."

Invoking Rudyard Kipling's poem "If," Blagojevich urged the public to exercise patience and withhold judgment until the facts emerge through criminal proceedings. He recited: "If you can keep your head when all about you are losing theirs and blaming it on you; if you can trust yourself when all men doubt you, but make allowance for their doubting, too; if you can wait and not be tired by waiting; or being lied about, don't deal in lies; or being hated, don't give way to hating."

# Illinois Governor Vows to Fight Corruption Allegations

CHICAGO (CNN) -- Rod Blagojevich, the governor caught in a political firestorm, declared on Friday that he would not step down from office and would battle the federal corruption charges against him, even as pressure mounted for his resignation following accusations that he tried to profit from selling the Senate seat vacated by President-elect Barack Obama.

Speaking briefly to journalists in Chicago without accepting any questions, the governor delivered an emotional statement: "I will fight, I will fight, I will fight until I take my last breath. I have done nothing wrong. I'm not going to quit a job that people have hired me to do."

This marked the first time the twice-elected governor had addressed the public regarding the scandal since federal agents arrested him on December 9th on corruption-related charges. According to government prosecutors, Blagojevich attempted to auction off Obama's vacant Senate position for personal gain. Additionally, authorities claim that both the governor and John Harris, his then-chief of staff, sought to pressure the Chicago Tribune into firing editorial board members by using state assistance to the Tribune Co.—the newspaper's parent company—as leverage during the company's sale of Wrigley Field.

Though eager to clear his name, Blagojevich indicated he would save detailed explanations for a more fitting venue rather than the media. "I'm not going to do what my accusers and political enemies have been doing, and that is talk about this case in 30-second sound bites on 'Meet the Press' or on the TV news," he stated. "I have on my side the most powerful ally there is, and it is the truth."

Referencing Rudyard Kipling's famous poem "If," the governor urged citizens to remain patient and withhold judgment until legal proceedings revealed all the facts. He recited lines from the poem about keeping composure amid accusations and maintaining trust despite others' doubts.

No questions were fielded during the press appearance. Prior to the event, defense attorney Ed Genson had indicated that responding to media inquiries wouldn't be wise for the governor at this stage. Genson has consistently maintained his client's innocence, further arguing that wiretap evidence gathered from Blagojevich's office and residence was obtained unlawfully.

The federal complaint—spanning 76 pages—contains excerpts from recorded phone conversations suggesting the governor's efforts to capitalize on the open Senate seat. Following the governor's remarks, Sam Adam Jr., serving as co-counsel alongside Genson, told reporters that prosecutors from the U.S. attorney's office had withheld crucial case materials. "We've been asking for the documents. We've been asking for the tapes. We've been asking for the witnesses, we're asking for a witness list. We have not gotten that," Adam explained.

The scandal has created significant turmoil within Illinois government, with numerous state leaders—Obama included—joining calls demanding the governor's departure. Harris, who faced his own corruption charges, stepped down from his position shortly following his arrest.

Meanwhile, a panel from the Illinois House of Representatives convened on Wednesday to continue evaluating whether sufficient grounds exist to pursue impeachment proceedings against Blagojevich.
